item.title: Haaland double helps Man City win, Neto brace cheers Chelsea
item.description: Argentina international Emi Martinez was taken to hospital following a clash of heads with Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite.
item.dc:creator: Martyn Herman
item.content:encoded: Manchester City bounced back from their midweek setback in Europe to maintain their perfect Premier League start with Erling Haaland's double propelling them to a 3-2 home win over battling Ipswich Town on Saturday. Paris St Germain inflicted a first meaningful defeat on Enzo Maresca's side in the Champions League on Wednesday but City shrugged off a gallant Ipswich side to make it seven wins from seven to cement their place at the top of the table. Chelsea beat Everton 2-0 in Saturday's early action thanks to Pedro Neto's brace although the London club's win was overshadowed by an injury to [USN:L4N46302T TEXT:"goalkeeper Emi Martinez"]. Liverpool came from a goal down to beat Brentford 2-1 away although they were helped by the previously unbeaten hosts being reduced to 10 men shortly before halftime when Yehor Yarmolyuk was shown a straight red card for a head butt. Manchester City have 21 points, six ahead of second-placed champions Arsenal, who visit Nottingham Forest on Sunday. Liverpool's win lifted them above Brentford into fifth place with 12 points behind Chelsea in fourth on 13. Third-placed Brighton & Hove Albion, who also have 13 points, host Crystal Palace on Sunday. Fulham moved off the foot of the table with their first league win of the season -- 1-0 at home to Hull City -- while Aston Villa won by the same scoreline at Newcastle United. BUSINESS AS USUAL FOR CITY Dark clouds remain over the Etihad Stadium with Manchester City's fate still unknown after they appealed a ruling that the club breached 114 Premier League financial rules. City have always denied any wrongdoing. But on the pitch it is very much business as usual, especially for Norwegian goal machine Haaland. Phil Foden gave City a short-lived lead cancelled out by Daizen Maeda, but Haaland restored the home side's advantage before halftime with a header from Mateo Kovacic's cross. Haaland then gave his side some breathing space with his second in the 69th minute, powering past Ipswich's Abdoul Ouattara before a low finish into the corner. He was denied a hat-trick by an offside decision and Ipswich got a lifeline when Zian Flemming tucked away a penalty in stoppage time but City bagged the points. The defiant mood was soured somewhat though as [USN:L8N46309A TEXT:"Haaland went off"] with an apparent injury late on, as did Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes and Nico O'Reilly, while Antoine Semenyo was also limping badly at the final whistle. "I don't know (Haaland's injury)," Maresca said. "I asked him. He said that he was okay. So hopefully, it's nothing serious." FEISTY FIRST HALF Chelsea have had a knack of scoring early this season but were kept at bay by hosts Everton in a feisty and physical first half that produced five yellow cards. However, Xabi Alonso's visitors needed just 43 seconds after the restart to go 1-0 up when Jorrel Hato cut the ball back from the byline to find Neto who swept home. Keeper Martinez's clash of heads with Jarrad Branthwaite resulted in the Argentine being strapped to a stretcher and taken off, leading to 11 minutes of stoppage time. Chelsea doubled their lead in the 90th minute when Neto pounced on a loose ball after Jordan Henderson's free kick was blocked by the wall, finding the bottom corner with a composed finish as Everton suffered their first defeat of the season. "What we know is he (Martinez) left the stadium conscious and right now he is in the hospital doing precautionary tests," Alonso said. "It was concussion but more than that I saw only one clip. Hopefully it won't be too bad but we need to wait." Martinez's knock gave 21-year-old keeper Mike Penders the chance to make his Premier League debut and he helped Chelsea keep a clean sheet in the league for the first time in 23 games. "We need a clean sheet, to be honest. I think we did a very good game. Emi deserved this, Mike did as well," Alonso added. BRENTFORD'S YARMOLYUK SENT OFF Liverpool deservedly fell behind at Brentford with Keane Lewis-Potter putting the hosts in front. Brentford were good value for their lead but Yarmolyuk's rush of blood to the head when he clashed with Jeremy Jacquet at a Liverpool corner changed the game. After referee John Brooks was invited to check a VAR monitor he brandished the red card at Ukrainian Yarmolyuk. Liverpool huffed and puffed after the break but Victor Munoz finally levelled in the 62nd minute when he cut in to beat keeper Caoimhin Kelleher with a left-foot finish. Alexander Isak won it for Andoni Iraola's side eight minutes later with a clinical strike from Bradley Barcola's assist. Brentford ended with nine men after Vitaly Janelt got a second yellow card for a foul on substitute Rio Ngumoha. Alex Iwobi's 33rd-minute strike for Fulham was enough to earn their new manager Alvaro Arbeloa a long-overdue league win and move Fulham up to 16th. Johan Manzambi's early goal secured Villa's victory at Newcastle, their second of the season.

item.title: Policía y manifestantes se enfrentan en uno de los peores episodios de disturbios en Francia en últimos años
item.description: Violentos enfrentamientos se dieron entre la policía y manifestantes en Francia, donde cientos de miles de personas se manifestaron contra el aumento de los precios y el deterioro de los servicios públicos, en lo que han sido algunos de los disturbios más destructivos que ha vivido el país en años.
item.dc:creator: Clotaire Achi, Janis Laizans
item.content:encoded: Violentos enfrentamientos se dieron entre la policía y manifestantes en Francia, donde cientos de miles de personas se manifestaron contra el aumento de los precios y el deterioro de los servicios públicos, en lo que han sido algunos de los disturbios más destructivos que ha vivido el país en años. El Ministerio del Interior informó de que al menos 272 personas habían sido detenidas tras incidentes violentos en los que participaron individuos encapuchados, entre otros lugares, en París, Marsella, en el sur, Toulouse, en el suroeste, Angers, en el oeste, y Lyon, en el centro-este de Francia. Bélgica, Portugal e Italia también se enfrentaron el sábado a protestas a menor escala debido al aumento del coste de la vida en Europa, mientras que en Albania los manifestantes volvieron a salir a la calle para protestar contra la supuesta corrupción del Gobierno, la falta de empleo y el bajo nivel de la educación. El primer ministro francés, Sébastien Lecornu, afirmó que el Gobierno no se dejaría "intimidar" por la violencia y atribuyó los disturbios a la "extrema izquierda" y a los delincuentes, a solo unos meses de las elecciones presidenciales del próximo año. "A aquellos que claramente quieren utilizar esta violencia como un “calentamiento” antes de las elecciones presidenciales, les digo con claridad: no nos dejaremos intimidar. Nadie impondrá su agenda política mediante la violencia", escribió en una publicación en X. El sindicato CGT declaró a la agencia de noticias Agence France-Presse que 800.000 personas en toda Francia habían participado en las protestas del sábado. El Ministerio del Interior no facilitó ninguna estimación, y la CGT no respondió a una solicitud de comentarios de Reuters. Los manifestantes afirmaron que la mayoría de la gente había marchado pacíficamente y atribuyeron gran parte de la violencia a alborotadores que se habían propuesto causar daños y enfrentarse a la policía. "Luchamos porque el coste de la vida es demasiado alto, porque el precio del combustible es demasiado elevado, porque los alumnos de secundaria están siendo atacados violentamente y resultando heridos por todo el país solo por intentar manifestarse y pedir más profesores y unas condiciones de aprendizaje dignas", afirmó Lola, una manifestante de 19 años en París. GAS LACRIMÓGENO, INCENDIOS Y SAQUEOS En algunas zonas de París, la policía lanzó ocasionalmente gases lacrimógenos mientras se replegaba ante una multitud de manifestantes, en su mayoría jóvenes, muchos de los cuales iban vestidos de negro y llevaban sudaderas con capucha, máscaras y gafas protectoras para protegerse del gas lacrimógeno. A última hora de la tarde, los manifestantes llegaron a lugares emblemáticos del centro de París, como los Campos Elíseos, la plaza de la Concordia y La Madeleine, que habían quedado excluidos del recorrido autorizado de la manifestación. El sábado por la noche, cuando las protestas iban remitiendo, los manifestantes incendiaron varios objetos, entre ellos al menos un coche. Se vio a algunos turistas en unos grandes almacenes de moda cerca de la Ópera de París tosiendo y escupiendo al quedar atrapados en las nubes de gas lacrimógeno, y las tiendas cercanas cerraron sus persianas a toda prisa. Se rompieron los escaparates de muchas tiendas y restaurantes de la capital, y se incendiaron coches y papeleras. En Lyon, los manifestantes incendiaron la oficina de turismo. En Marsella, el alcalde afirmó que el ayuntamiento había sido objeto de actos vandálicos y que se estaban enviando refuerzos policiales a la ciudad tras las conversaciones mantenidas con el Gobierno. En unas protestas inspiradas en parte por las de Francia, varios cientos de personas, en su mayoría jóvenes, se manifestaron en Bruselas, y algunas se enfrentaron a la policía. Grupos de estudiantes belgas han afirmado que protestan contra el aumento de los costes de la educación y contra unas reformas que, según temen, harán que la educación superior sea menos accesible. En Albania, la policía disparó lo que parecían ser balas de goma contra los manifestantes durante el quinto día de manifestaciones estudiantiles masivas en las que se pedía la dimisión del primer ministro Edi Rama. En Portugal, decenas de miles de personas salieron a las calles de Lisboa tras varios días de disturbios para protestar contra los precios de la vivienda y otros costes de la vida. Los precios de la vivienda en Portugal se han duplicado desde 2017, lo que ha agravado una de las peores crisis de asequibilidad de Europa. En Italia, una marcha contra el elevado coste de la vida en Milán degeneró en disturbios, y la policía despejó la plaza central de la catedral con gas lacrimógeno. La policía de Bolonia utilizó cañones de agua para intentar dispersar a la multitud y detuvo a siete personas después de que otra protesta se tornara violenta, según informó la agencia de noticias ANSA. LA RESPUESTA DE LA POLICÍA FRANCESA, BAJO LA LUPA Las protestas en Francia comenzaron el mes pasado en institutos de los suburbios pobres del norte de París, donde la indignación por la falta de profesores y las instalaciones precarias se convirtió en un movimiento más amplio centrado en la desigualdad, el gasto público y el nivel de vida. El sábado, en París, manifestantes con chalecos de alta visibilidad bloquearon las calles, recordando el movimiento de los "chalecos amarillos» que marcó el anterior mandato del presidente Emmanuel Macron. Macron, que el viernes instó a la calma, entra en la recta final de su presidencia, enfrentándose a un panorama político fragmentado y a una presión creciente en materia económica. Los esfuerzos de Francia por reducir la deuda pública no han logrado tranquilizar a los inversionistas, lo que ha elevado los costos de financiación del Estado a sus niveles más altos en más de dos décadas. Las tácticas policiales han suscitado críticas tras los heridos entre los manifestantes, entre ellos un adolescente que perdió una mano tras recoger una granada aturdidora. Lecornu señaló que más de 900 agentes de policía también habían resultado heridos en protestas anteriores. El organismo de control policial está investigando al menos dos docenas de denuncias de violencia policial. La policía lanzó gases lacrimógenos y se enfrentó a los manifestantes en varias ciudades francesas el sábado, cuando algunas de las protestas más violentas de los últimos años, motivadas por el costo de la vida y los servicios públicos, llevaron a miles de personas a las calles. Las autoridades francesas indicaron que, a mediodía, se habían registrado 140 manifestaciones en las que participaron 32.800 personas fuera de París, y achacaron los disturbios a lo que describieron como la "ultraizquierda". Las protestas comenzaron el mes pasado en institutos de los suburbios pobres del norte de París, donde la indignación por la falta de profesores y el mal estado de las instalaciones se convirtió en un movimiento más amplio centrado en la desigualdad, el gasto público y el nivel de vida. Se registraron incidentes violentos en varias ciudades, entre ellos actos de vandalismo en Marsella y ataques dirigidos contra la policía, los medios de comunicación y edificios públicos, según informó el Ministerio del Interior. Se observó una fuerte presencia policial en el centro de París, especialmente cerca de lugares emblemáticos como los Campos Elíseos y el Arco del Triunfo, que quedaron excluidos de los recorridos de las dos manifestaciones autorizadas. Los manifestants, ataviados con chalecos de alta visibilidad, bloquearon las calles, lo que recordó al movimiento de los "chalecos amarillos" que marcó el anterior mandato del presidente Emmanuel Macron. En Marsella, el alcalde afirmó que el ayuntamiento había sido objeto de actos de vandalismo y que se estaban enviando refuerzos policiales a la ciudad tras las conversaciones mantenidas con el primer ministro y el ministro del Interior. "Luchamos porque el costo de la vida es demasiado elevado, porque el precio del combustible es demasiado alto, porque los alumnos de secundaria están siendo atacados violentamente y resultando heridos por todo el país solo por intentar manifestarse y pedir más profesores y unas condiciones de aprendizaje dignas", afirmó Lola, una manifestante de 19 años en París. Macron, que el viernes instó a la calma, entra en la recta final de su presidencia en medio de un panorama político fragmentado y una presión creciente sobre la economía. Los esfuerzos de Francia por reducir la deuda pública no han logrado tranquilizar a los inversionistas, lo que ha llevado los costos de financiación del Estado a sus niveles más altos en más de dos décadas. RESPUESTA POLICIAL BAJO ESCRUTINIO Las tácticas policiales han suscitado críticas tras una serie de heridos entre los manifestantes, entre ellos un adolescente que perdió una mano tras recoger una granada aturdidora. El primer ministro, Sébastien Lecornu, afirmó que también habían resultado heridos más de 900 agentes de policía. El organismo de control policial está investigando al menos dos docenas de denuncias de violencia policial. Francia suspendió el uso de granadas aturdidoras durante las manifestaciones estudiantiles, pero el ministro del Interior, Laurent Núñez, afirmó que podrían utilizarse el sábado. Las convocatorias en las redes sociales para que los veteranos de movimientos de protesta anteriores se unieran a las manifestaciones parecen haber ampliado la participación, lo que aumenta la posibilidad de que estas alcancen una mayor envergadura. El movimiento de los Chalecos Amarillos surgió en 2018 en oposición a los impuestos sobre el diésel, antes de ampliarse a una protesta más general contra el costo de la vida y la desigualdad.

item.title: Albanian police fire rubber bullets as student protests rage
item.description: Pellets hit two Reuters journalists and several protesters, leaving marks.
item.dc:creator: Fatos Bytyci
item.content:encoded: Police in Albania fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters on Saturday, the fifth day of mass student demonstrations demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama step down. Reuters video footage showed police firing a shotgun towards crowds outside the education ministry during clashes with protesters. Reuters reporters found rubber pellets on the ground and pellets hit two Reuters journalists and several protesters, leaving round marks. The incident marks an escalation in a confrontation between police and protesters that has engulfed central Tirana in recent days. Demonstrators have burned government buildings and banks and hurled rocks at police, who have responded with tear gas and water cannon. Albania's police chief Skender Hita did not deny the use of rubber bullets when asked about it at a news conference on Saturday. "All means that were used were employed in a limited manner, including the most recent ones," he said. Hita said seven police officers have been suspended and were facing disciplinary investigations for "exceeding their authority" and "failure to respect the principle of proportionality" in dealing with protesters. He did not specify the incidents that led to the suspensions. The demonstrations have been fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards. They have also drawn support from people who felt ignored during a summer of largely peaceful protest against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner. The unrest poses the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who last year won a fourth term in office. "It's been 13 years of corruption and 13 years of doing nothing and empty promises. So the jar is filled and we are here for our rights," said Juri Taullahu, a 22-year-old medical student, on Saturday. Police and the government condemned the unrest and called for calm. Hita said that 1,067 people had been arrested and 388 criminally prosecuted. Scores of police officers and protesters have been injured. KUSHNER-BACKED RESORT TRIGGERED SUMMER PROTESTS Rama's administration has been dogged by corruption scandals, while analysts say Albania has become a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drug and weapons trafficking, complicating the country's efforts to join the European Union. Villagers told Reuters in July that their land had been [USN:L6N42J18T TEXT:"wrongfully sold"] for the Kushner-backed development on a pristine stretch of coast in southern Albania. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was [USN:L6N4380FB TEXT:"wanted by prosecutors"] on suspicion of drug trafficking, accusations his lawyer denied. Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute. Rama, who denies wrongdoing and told Reuters this week that he would not step down, said on Saturday that his government respected the students and their right to protest. "My responsibility is even clearer during these difficult times ... to protect our citizens, guarantee justice, and move Albania forward — together with this governing majority, which holds a very clear mandate: to see Albania in the European Union by 2030," he said on Facebook. Along with Montenegro, Albania is leading the EU accession process among Balkan countries. Albania's unrest coincides with growing street protests elsewhere in Europe. In France, student [USN:L1N46302B TEXT:"protests"] demanding more teachers and better facilities have spread into a broader wave of unrest. Spain has seen protests against high rents and a lack of housing, prompting the government to call a [USN:L8N46011N TEXT:"snap election"].

item.title: Davidovich Fokina beats Zverev, sets up all-Spanish Shanghai final with Jodar
item.description: Davidovich Fokina secured only his second win over Zverev in eight meetings.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Alejandro Davidovich Fokina upset top seed Alexander Zverev 5-7 6-4 6-3 on Saturday to reach the Shanghai Masters final, where he was joined by fellow Spaniard Rafael Jodar after the 20-year-old sensation downed former world number one Daniil Medvedev. Davidovich Fokina, the 25th seed, fired 36 winners in the two-hour, two-minute contest to secure only his second victory over Zverev in eight meetings. His previous win against the German came in the round of 32 at the Canadian Open in 2023. He earned his first break of the match to take the second set, forcing a decider with a stunning backhand passing shot on the run that capped a bruising baseline exchange and brought the crowd to their feet. Carrying that momentum into the final set, Davidovich Fokina broke Zverev for a 2-0 lead and never relinquished control, booking a place in the second ATP Masters 1000 final of his career after finishing runner-up in Monte Carlo in 2022. Landing 82% of his first serves and repeatedly exposing Zverev on the forehand side, the 27-year-old secured one of the biggest victories of his career. "I knew that if I stayed there all match, I could get at least one chance and I took it there in the second set," Davidovich Fokina said. "Then in the third set, I think I was better physically. The early break in the third set gave me a lot of power. "I focused on just playing, not mattering about the result but enjoying." Davidovich Fokina has now won nine consecutive matches in China after lifting his second tour-level title at the ATP 250 event in Chengdu last month. It was a disappointing end to the week for Zverev, a seven-time ATP Masters 1000 champion whose best result in Shanghai remains his runner-up finish to Medvedev in 2019. The 29-year-old has otherwise enjoyed a fine season, ending his Grand Slam drought at the [USN:L1N42F08C TEXT:"French Open"] before claiming a second major title at the [USN:L6N4550DD TEXT:"US Open"] and securing the ATP [USN:L1N45Y0DG TEXT:"year-end world number one"] ranking after Jannik [USN:L1N45S0CV TEXT:"Sinner was sidelined"] for the remainder of the season with a knee injury. Twelfth seed Jodar continued his remarkable rise by becoming the youngest Shanghai finalist in tournament history and strengthening his chances of qualifying for the ATP Finals in his first full season on the tour with a 6-3 6-4 victory over fifth-seeded Russian Medvedev. The aggressive right-hander, who was ranked outside the world's top 900 little more than a year ago, is seeking the second ATP title of his career after capturing his maiden crown in Morocco and will now compete in his first Masters 1000 final. "It was a very tough match," Jodar said. "In the first set all the games were very close, with breakpoints for him, breakpoints for me. "I'm super happy with how I handled the important moments in the first set, and also how I returned and served. "Daniil is always a very tough player. I think he played great today. So I had to be at my best level to beat him." Sunday's championship match will mark the first meeting between Jodar and Davidovich Fokina.

item.title: Chuck Lorre on his reign as the ‘King of Sitcoms’
item.description: Laughter, Chuck Lorre is keen to point out, is not a voluntary act. It is not something we choose, but something that happens to us, like an unexpected gift.
item.dc:creator: Yasmeen Serhan
item.content:encoded: American television producer Chuck Lorre poses for a portrait at Warner Bros. Studios in Burbank, California, US, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Daniel Cole Laughter, Chuck Lorre is keen to point out, is not a voluntary act. It is not something we choose, but something that happens to us, like an unexpected gift. Lorre knows something about making it happen. Dubbed the “King of Sitcoms,” he has spent decades making audiences laugh, from his early work as a writer on the hit comedy “Roseanne” to creating shows, including “The Big Bang Theory,” “Two and a Half Men,” “Mom,” and “Mike & Molly.” In his newly released memoir, “Sitcom,” Lorre turns that comic instinct on his own life, writing candidly about his missteps, while also looking back at the television successes and creative battles that shaped his career. Speaking with Reuters from Los Angeles, he discusses why character is key to great comedy, what he learned from getting things wrong, and why he’s optimistic about the TV industry’s future. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. The memoir is very funny despite tackling difficult subjects, from failed marriages to addiction and Scientology. What made you want to open up about them now? From the outset, I was trying to write it as if I was having a conversation with somebody. Rather than reporting or reiterating stuff, I was trying to write it as if I was talking to the audience or talking to a person; more conversational as opposed to you know, being locked up in the prose of it all. I've been talking about these crazy chapters of my life for a long time and dear friend nudged me for at least two years to start writing it down. And once I started writing it down, I was quite pleasantly surprised. I realized it was cathartic. It was it was a little bit of therapy for me. Having finished the darned thing, what became really clear was all the missteps I've made in my life were all necessary for me to arrive at where I am, and I am deeply grateful for where I am. So the path may have been bumpy, but that's what was required. What most excites you about television right now, and what terrifies you? There's plenty in this world that is terrifying, but I wouldn't put TV in that category. Actually, I'm an optimist about how the business is changing. I've heard people complain that there's too many choices. And to me that's like, really? Does that mean when you walk into a supermarket, you complain that there's too many choices? That's got to be a good thing. When I came up in this in television, there was three and a half networks. Fox was just starting. And that was it. If those three said no, it's simply not going to happen. Now there's I don't know how many platforms capable of helping a writer (or) performer create something and perhaps get it seen by a legitimate audience. Of all the shows you’ve created, which felt most miraculous? Probably Big Bang. I mean, the first pilot was an abject failure, with the exception of (co-stars) Johnny Galecki and Jim Parsons. I had to wrap my head around the fact that it was poorly written and, when we were given another opportunity one year later, we got a chance to write a better pilot. You don't get do-overs in this business, but we did. I didn't understand what we were creating till we created it. I didn't understand how viscerally the audience was going to connect with these outliers, these brilliant but incompetent characters. What makes a great comedy? It's really very simple. It's about characters. Well-designed, thought out characters, portrayed by the right actor. I adored "Cheers" and "Seinfeld" and "Everybody Loves Raymond," "Archie Bunker," Norman Lear's stuff. I wasn't watching for the plot. The storytelling of it was secondary. It was these extraordinary characters that I loved and I wanted to see them every week. And that's how I've always approached creating television shows. Character, character, character. I don't think I could sit here and remember one storyline for "Cheers," but I never missed an episode because I wanted to see those characters. Those characters made me laugh. And I think that's the secret sauce for comedy. Obviously, when you work in the drama world, plotting is an entirely different thing. You're watching for the adventure, the hero's journey. That's a story. But even in that world, which I know very little about, I'm thinking about character. Going back to the importance of casting, you write about the resistance you faced casting Melissa McCarthy in “Mike & Molly,” with one network executive pushing for a slimmer actress. How much has the industry changed, and how did you learn which battles were worth fighting? Well, the good news is, because I've had some success, I don't have that many battles anymore. But it took a long time for me to fight for who I believed in as opposed to being a good soldier and taking direction. I learned the hard way that when you do what you're told to do by others and you fail, it's your failure. It's not theirs. At a certain point, I started to dig my heels in and I think first and most formidably (was) with Jon Cryer. I talk about how much resistance I got from CBS to cast Jon in "Two and a Half Men" and then Melissa McCarthy. Here was a generational talent and it was "over my dead body" kind of casting. And I went, "Fine, well, produce a dead body because we're going over it." I guess what I'm trying to say is, it took me a while to find the courage to fight these fights. I didn't have it in the beginning. I was too frightened about being tossed aside and sent home. How concerned are you about AI in the writers’ room? Are the protections won in the 2023 writers’ strike enough? There's plenty of reason to be concerned about this technology. Television would be the least of it, I would think. Why is that? I just think, if we're going to prioritize our concerns, for me AI is concerning in that it could topple civilization, not take away jobs on sitcoms, not that that's not important. But creating an intelligence that so wildly surpasses human intelligence is an incredibly risky endeavor. Look what we've done as the apex predator on this planet. Imagine what would happen if there was an apex-apex predator that viewed us the way we view insects. That scares me. Do you expect to see more shows tapping into those fears? We did an episode on "Stuart Fails to Save the Universe" with an AI overlord that has shock collars around everyone so when they get angry or contentious and asocial, they're shocked into submission. You write that good TV writing starts with reading good writing. What happens to television if people are reading less? I really love words. I love the meaning of words, the sound of words, the music of words. And comedy, from my perspective, is really absolutely correct use of words to cause a response; to cause laughter. And laughter happens to you. Real laughter is involuntary. It should surprise the laugher. And that's a result of both words and images. I guess I could be concerned about a future where words become less relevant because they're my favorite things. Finally, some quick-fire questions. If you had to cast someone to portray you, who would you insist on? Idris Elba. No? Maybe not. (laughs) Why would you even ask that question? Are we going to make a movie out of the book? You never know! If you could revisit one of your shows, which would it be? "Dharma and Greg." I've always felt a profound regret for having left. There was so much more to explore, but I didn't know how. What’s your comfort watch? I really am drawn to dramas. I like to watch what I don't do. I love "Slow Horses" and "Furious." "Lucky" was another thing I saw and really enjoyed. "The Diplomat" is (also) terrific. As far as current comedies are concerned, if I want to laugh, I watch John Oliver and Jon Stewart. They absolutely know how to make me laugh out loud. The perspectives expressed in Culture Current are the subject’s own and do not necessarily reflect the views of Reuters News.

item.title: Exotic species appear off California thanks to an unusually strong El Niño
item.description: The weather pattern is bringing warm Pacific Ocean water farther north, and tropical species with it
item.dc:creator: Daniel Trotta, Matt Silverstein
item.content:encoded: The longfin bigeye fish was spotted in California for the first time last month, and the first sea turtles of any kind nested on California beaches. Meanwhile, a venomous yellow-bellied sea snake swam ashore as whale sharks and hammerheads cruised just off the coast. Exotic species have been visiting California's shores since an unusually strong El Niño weather phenomenon arrived this year. Occurring naturally every few years, El Niño brings warm ocean water farther north, and tropical species with it, providing California with a stunning visual display that has become ever more evident with the advent of drone and video technology. "There's kind of a buzz. Fishermen are loving it for sure. I'm as interested as anybody else. It's strange times," said Nate Jaros, vice president of animal care at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach. Other visitors include flying fish and manta rays. California had already experienced an unusual marine heat wave just before its arrival. This year's phenomenon coincided with a string of hurricanes in the eastern Pacific, fueling sea level rise and large waves that have [USN:L6N45D11J TEXT:"destroyed homes and denuded some Southern California beaches"] of sand. Preparing for more effects to come this winter, California has declared a state of emergency. But it has provided a bounty for businesses like Dana Wharf Sportfishing & Whale Watching. Co-owner Donna Kalez said anglers have pulled in 5,000 yellowfin tuna this year, compared to 2 a year ago. They are also landing wahoo and dorado, also known as mahi-mahi, a green fish with a blunt head giving it the profile of a bulldozer. "Dorado is very exciting because they're very acrobatic, so they jump out of the water. We catch them off kelp paddies, and it's a thrill," Kalez said. Experts expect conditions to mostly return to normal after El Niño, a natural phenomenon predating human-caused climate change, passes next year. The greatest short-term harm may be to kelp, which thrives in colder waters and provides habitat for multiple species, experts say. "It’s good for some sharks and probably bad for others," said Chris Lowe, director of the Shark Lab at California State University, Long Beach. "For animals that can't move, that's a bigger problem, right? Most sharks that are highly mobile. They can simply move." The yellow-bellied sea snake may have venomous fangs but cannot swim like a large shark. When an apparently sick one swam ashore in Orange County in September, a beachgoer used a palm frond to lift it off the sand and drop it in the sea. Jaros said that based on cellphone video he had little doubt it was the yellow-bellied sea snake, Hydrophis platurus. There have only been six or seven confirmed sightings in California, said William Ludt, associate curator of ichthyology at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County. The last confirmed sighting came during the El Niño of 2015-2016, he said. Exotic sharks such as the whale shark — a gentle giant and the largest fish on Earth — and the more menacing-looking hammerheads venture into California waters during El Niño. Both have been spotted recently. Lowe said a white shark nursery reappeared for the first time since 2011 in Santa Monica Bay, where juveniles frolic without bothering humans. Ludt said the aptly named longfin bigeye fish species was recorded for the first time in California this year when an angler caught one on the Venice Fishing Pier in Los Angeles. When two olive ridley sea turtle nests were found on a pair of Orange County beaches in September, they marked the first-ever recorded nest for any sea turtle species on the US West Coast, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The first was discovered by a beachgoer in Seal Beach on September 16, the second by lifeguards in neighboring Huntington Beach three days later, officials said. And other new species may yet arrive. "We still aren't fully through it," Ludt said. "It's still very much ongoing."

item.title: Trump-Zelenskiy rift threatens vital support for Kyiv
item.description: Their relationship had steadied until Ukraine's strikes on energy sites in Russia began contributing to rising fuel prices, a political headache for President Trump ahead of the midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Simon Lewis, Steve Holland, Daniel Flynn
item.content:encoded: From US threats to cut off intelligence support for Ukraine to a waiver of tariffs on Russian exports and a [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"diesel deal"] that could help Russia fund its war, it has been a damaging week for ties between Kyiv and its most important ally, Washington. US President Donald Trump, frustrated by high energy costs he blames partly on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, has repeatedly criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. A disruption of US-provided satellite internet services raised fears that Ukraine could be vulnerable as it prepares for another [USN:L6N4620NO TEXT:"winter of Russian attacks"] on its energy infrastructure. Zelenskiy responded to Trump's barbs with an [USN:L8N4620FR TEXT:"unusually sharp"] series of public criticisms of Trump, suggesting the US was now favoring Russia. He said Ukraine would defy Trump's demand to stop striking Russian energy targets, citing Russia's continued attacks. Intensifying the discord, Trump [USN:L1N463009 TEXT:"waived key US Russia-related sanctions and tariffs"] on Friday, shortly before they were scheduled to take effect. That prompted Zelenskiy to say in social media posts that Trump's action would encourage Russia to continue attacks on Ukraine. The widening rift has sparked concerns that Trump and Zelenskiy's tumultuous relationship could lead to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. Trump could yet restrict the supply of weapons to Ukraine, follow through on threats to stop sharing battlefield intelligence, or strike more economic deals with Moscow. Despite Zelenskiy's remarks, Kyiv wants to continue dialogue with Trump's envoys, his friend Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks said, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Denys Sienik, chargé d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, told Newsmax on Friday that Ukraine was grateful to Trump and his team for their efforts to end the war and said Ukraine was willing to engage in talks with Russia. Trump told reporters on Friday he would continue to deal with both Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “I want that war to end,” he said. 'MISSED OPPORTUNITY': FORMER US OFFICIAL Daniel Fried, the senior State Department official on Europe from 2005 to 2009, said it was unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine, but the fallout was damaging prospects for an end to the war that began with Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion. "It's not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it's not cost-free," said Fried, now at the Washington-based Atlantic Council think tank. Trump's relationship with Zelenskiy has long been uneasy. Trump and US Vice President JD Vance publicly upbraided Zelenskiy during an Oval Office meeting in February 2025. Washington has paused or slowed military assistance to Ukraine under Trump, while allowing European allies to purchase US weapons for Kyiv. The relationship had steadied until Ukraine's strikes this year on energy sites in Russia began contributing to rising fuel prices. High gasoline and diesel prices are a political headache for Trump ahead of November's midterm elections, in which his Republican Party could lose its majorities in the US Congress, according to analysts. Experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran , which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz. Frustrated by Zelenskiy, however, Trump turned to Russia to increase fuel supply and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal debate, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel. In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump also waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs shortly before they were supposed to take effect under the Graham Act, which Trump signed last month. Although the law, named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, called for new penalties on Russia starting next week, it also allows the president to waive them if it is in the US national interest to do so. Zelenskiy said Trump's latest action undercuts the Graham Act's main goal and will fuel Russia's "desire to keep killing people." The US diesel deal with Russia and the waiver are the latest steps in what Zelenskiy said he expects to be continued sanctions relief on Moscow. The prospect of the US continuing to pressure Russia to end the war has dimmed since Graham's death in July, Zelenskiy said. Graham, a South Carolina Republican and a confidant of Trump, strongly supported Ukraine. "It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest," the Ukrainian president wrote. HIGH STAKES FOR UKRAINE For Kyiv, the stakes are high and immediate. Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a deadly [USN:L4N45Z20E TEXT:"Russian attack"] on the capital. Without US intelligence, Ukraine could face greater difficulty detecting and countering Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly against energy infrastructure that Moscow has repeatedly targeted during previous winters. Trump has said the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. But Zelenskiy told NPR that US officials had warned Ukrainian commanders intelligence could be reduced or cut off. Ukraine's Starshield system, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink service, was [USN:L8N46213X TEXT:"disrupted"] after what two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said was [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"an order originating from the White House"], Reuters reported on Thursday. The service has been partially restored, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability created by Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by US companies and subject to decisions by the Trump administration. Trump may face resistance if congressional Republicans see his approach as weakening Ukraine while benefiting Russia. Ukraine retains support among Trump's fellow Republicans, some of whom [USN:L1N45Z0TJ TEXT:"argue that"] Washington should not pressure Kyiv into accepting a settlement on terms favorable to Moscow. Zelenskiy's tough responses to Trump were risky, but he may be counting on a power shift on Capitol Hill after the midterm elections to make it harder for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia and further reduce military assistance to Kyiv, said Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and head of the Global Situation Room consultancy. “Zelenskiy knows who he’s dealing with,” he said. “Trump’s threats don’t have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office.”

item.title: Hargeisa like a local
item.description: Our digital journalist’s guide to camel milk tea, bustling markets and mobile money.
item.dc:creator: Hani Richter
item.content:encoded: REUTERS/Illustration/Kate Evans “Resilience is victory,” goes a famous Somali proverb, and few places embody it like Hargeisa. Turned to rubble by intense bombings during a decade-long war with Somalia, this Somaliland city was rebuilt through domestic grit and community labour. Somaliland, a breakaway region of Somalia that has enjoyed effective autonomy since it declared independence in 1991, is my home away from home. It is where my mother spent her early childhood and where some of my extended family still live. Though I was born in Bonn, Germany, and grew up in London, where I joined Reuters as a social media editor in 2019, I have regularly visited Hargeisa. Every time, I wish I had stayed longer. Hargeisa translates as “the place where hides are sold” in Somali, and livestock remains the backbone of the economy, alongside remittances. But it is also a city where old meets new: People buy and sell lambs and goats through their phones, using mobile money to pay for food, clothing and much else. Here’s how to experience Hargeisa like a local: Getting around: Somaliland is a devoutly Muslim place where days start early, with the first call to prayer before sunrise acting as a natural alarm for many residents. Walking is a great way to take in the atmosphere of the city. Though be warned: Roads and driving can be chaotic. Everyone is in a rush, so be aware of your surroundings and be mindful of manoeuvring cars, buses, motorbikes and even the occasional determined man with a wheelbarrow. People shop at an open-air market along a street in Hargeisa, Somaliland, a breakaway region of Somalia that has enjoyed effective autonomy since it declared independence in 1991. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A Soviet-made MiG-17 fighter jet, formerly belonging to the Somali Air Force, sits atop the Hargeisa War Memorial monument in the Freedom Square along Independence Avenue. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A trader pours camel milk at an open-air milk bar. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A trader handles camel milk from a steel can at an open-air milk bar. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A man stands next to second-hand clothes for sale at an open-air stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Traders wait for customers as they sell second-hand clothes. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A woman waits for customers at her open-air butchery. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A trader displays mobile phones for sale at an open-air stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Vehicles parked outside Durdur Business Center, along Road No 1, 26 June District. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A woman uses her mobile phone as she walks past the New Moon restaurant. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A man uses a sewing machine at his tailoring stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Shoes are displayed for sale at the Kaboole fashion store. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed People sit along a street in Hargeisa. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A man sits inside the Muddakar coffee house restaurant. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A woman sells fruit at an open-air grocery stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed People sit at a coffee shop. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Traffic along a street in Hargeisa. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed For a more local experience, take a minibus. It’s a hail and ride system, so just flag down the bus as you would a taxi, confirm it’s going to your destination, and let the driver know when you want to get off. Note that they can often be crowded. For journeys outside of the centre, take a taxi or Dhaweeye, which translates as “closer” in English. They are always nearby and easily flagged off the street. Mobile money is king: As is the case in many African cities, mobile money is the preferred payment method in Hargeisa and to pay for anything you will need your phone. You don't need internet access; just ask which code to use and for the vendor's number. You can also pay with cash, of course, but it may take a bit longer. What to eat and drink: Many people make a living by selling their wares on the street. As you walk around the city, you will be called into restaurants and street stalls, where fruit sellers pile watermelons as tall as a person, and vendors fry potatoes. Camel meat and camel milk are must-tries. Somalis have been eating camel for centuries, a tradition rooted in the land’s arid landscape. When crops and cattle perished, camels were the only ones to survive. For a traditional snack on the go, try dried camel meat, called muqmaad. Walking is a great way to take in the atmosphere of the city. Though be warned: Roads and driving can be chaotic. For breakfast , people enjoy stir-fried goat, lamb or beef liver with Somali pancakes (lahoox), or a flaky flatbread with honey that goes well with shaax, a spiced, aromatic tea made with camel milk that tastes very similar to chai. A favourite lunch is fragrant Somali rice (bariis) and meat, typically tender, bone-in goat or lamb — with a banana on the side. Tea is at the heart of social life in Hargeisa, and you will regularly see people sitting outside tea houses, drinking and talking politics. With Ethiopia next door, you are never far from a good cup of coffee either. Try Social Cafe, one of several cafes in the city or, for a Somali twist, order Qaxwo, made with spices such as ginger, cinnamon and cardamom. City landmarks: The Hargeisa War Memorial features a downed Somali Air Force MiG-17 aircraft. Located in Freedom Square, it is probably the city's most recognisable landmark. The livestock market offers a glimpse into one of the city's main economic drivers, and is particularly interesting if you have never experienced the pastoral side of Somali culture. You’ll see large numbers of goats, sheep and camels being sold. Go in the morning to see it at its busiest. If you are looking for entertainment, stop by the Hiddo Dhawr Cultural Centre. Founded in 2013 by Somali singer and activist Sahra Halgan, it often features live performances of Somali music and poetry. For an authentic shopping experience, visit the Waheen Market, the city's main commercial market, where you will find everything from mattresses and glassware to gold jewellery. It’s also a great place to pick up a souvenir. One popular option is a dhill, a traditional wooden vessel used to store milk, usually adorned with leather straps and cowrie shells. Another is frankincense, an aromatic resin. Somaliland is one of the few places in the world where frankincense grows naturally. The gum is chewed for its health benefits, while the resin is traditionally burned to freshen homes and welcome guests. Finally, no visit to Hargeisa is complete without a trip to the money market, a famous open-air street market where vendors trade bricks of local currency and US dollars. There are piles of cash as far as the eye can see — but with mobile money now the first choice, who knows how long it will be there. Dress like a local: Hargeisa is a conservative place where people dress modestly. To fit in, try sporting some traditional dress. Women wear beautiful dresses called baatis with matching hijabs, often in tie-dye or other intricate designs, while men wear a sarong wrap decorated with traditional prints. When to visit: If you are visiting during the summer months, when it is hottest, expect average temperatures of around 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit) during the day. In winter, temperatures reach about 26 C (79 F) at their highest, which is considered cool. CITY MEMO DATA POINTS Population : 1.3 million Price of a cup of tea : $0.20 to $1.50. My go-to spot for breakfast or lunch is CFC. Great place to watch the sunset : Sarovar Hotel is located at the top of a mountain and offers an unforgettable view of Hargeisa. Largest university : University of Hargeisa, more than 7,000 students

item.title: Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital
item.description: Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital samedi après-midi pour regagner le Vatican, quatre jours après avoir subi une intervention chirurgicale pour un cancer du poumon.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital samedi après-midi pour regagner le Vatican, quatre jours après avoir subi une intervention chirurgicale pour un cancer du poumon. Le souverain pontife, âgé de 71 ans, s'est rendu sans aide jusqu'à la voiture qui l'attendait, s'arrêtant pour saluer les fidèles rassemblés devant l'hôpital Gemelli de Rome. Ses médecins avaient précédemment indiqué qu'il se sentait suffisamment bien pour rentrer chez lui après avoir effectué les dernières analyses sanguines et examens d'imagerie thoracique. Le pape, qui a subi mardi une opération visant à lui retirer le lobe inférieur du poumon droit, fera dimanche sa première apparition publique depuis son intervention pour prononcer la traditionnelle prière de l'Angélus sur la place Saint-Pierre, a confirmé le Saint-Siège. Léon a reçu un diagnostic d’adénocarcinome pulmonaire, la forme la plus courante de cancer du poumon. Ce diagnostic, pour un pape connu pour être relativement jeune et énergique et qui n’a été élu qu’en mai 2025, a provoqué un choc et soulevé des questions quant à l’avenir de son pontificat alors qu’il doit faire face à la maladie. Les médecins du pape ont indiqué que son opération s’était déroulée avec succès, sans complications. Ils n’ont toutefois pas encore révélé la taille de la tumeur ni précisé si la maladie s’était propagée aux ganglions lymphatiques voisins, deux facteurs essentiels pour établir le pronostic.

item.title: Pope Leo returns to Vatican four days after cancer surgery
item.description: A smiling Pope Leo left hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican four days after surgery for lung cancer, an illness that has prompted speculation about how his 17-month papacy might change.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee
item.content:encoded: A smiling Pope Leo left hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican four days after surgery for lung cancer, an illness that has prompted speculation about how his 17-month papacy might change. The pope walked unaided to his waiting car, waving to well-wishers outside Rome's Gemelli Hospital. He stopped to speak to a 13-year-old girl named Varvara from Ukraine who has been in Italy for cancer treatment. Leo, 71, was pictured smiling broadly and waving through an open window when his black SUV left the hospital grounds. He appeared in good spirits as he left the hospital in video released by the Vatican. He shook hands with a group of Franciscan friars, one of whom said: "This is the second time (we have met). Let's hope there will be a third and fourth." The pope laughed and replied: "Many times, but not for these reasons." PRAYERS ON SUNDAY His doctors had said earlier on Saturday that he was well enough to return home after they carried out the latest blood tests and chest imaging, and that he was able to perform normal daily activities independently. Leo, who had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, will hold his first public engagement since surgery when he will lead weekly prayers with pilgrims from his apartment overlooking St. Peter's Square at noon (1000 GMT) on Sunday. He has been diagnosed with [USN:L8N46006S TEXT:"lung adenocarcinoma"], the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and [USN:L8N4600P9 TEXT:"raised questions"] about the future shape of his papacy. The pope's doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications. They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis. SOUTH AMERICAN TRIP Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the pope's lead surgeon, said that Leo could be fully recovered in another 10 days and that there was no reason to call off his planned visit to South America next month. "As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place," he told the Vatican News website. Leo is planning to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a pope [USN:L8N45D0VL TEXT:"in decades"]. Margaritora said the tumour had been discovered by chance during what he called a routine abdominal examination. The Vatican signaled on Friday that Leo, known for following a busy schedule, intended to keep up his commitments, as some cardinals began to publicly express concern about the pope's health. In a sign the pope was back to work, Leo held a phone call on Friday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, [USN:L8N4621IK TEXT:"urging a ceasefire"] to help get vital supplies into Oleshky, a Russian-controlled Ukrainian town. Lebanese pilgrim Abdul Halim Fatha was in St. Peter's Square as Leo arrived back at the Vatican and expressed sadness over the pope's cancer diagnosis. "But I know God will be with him and protect him," he said.

item.title: AI rapidly improving, could vastly boost US GDP, Anthropic's Clark tells policymakers
item.description: BANGKOK, Oct 17 : Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50 per cent by
item.dc:creator: CNA
item.content:encoded:

AI rapidly improving, could vastly boost US GDP, Anthropic's Clark tells policymakers

Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark attends "AI and the Global Economy: From Risk to Opportunity" at the IMF/World Bank 2026 Annual Meetings at Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok, Thailand, October 16, 2026. REUTERS/Patipat Janthong

FAST

BANGKOK, Oct 17 : Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50 per cent by 2030. Clark, speaking at IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, said that international cooperation was needed to erect "unusual and serious rules" for the transformative technology, and there was a shrinking window for policymakers to act. Clark said that the estimated potential US GDP of $44 trillion, which compares to the current level of just over $30 trillion, "sounds very outlandish, I know." But he added that AI was vastly increasing scientific discovery. He said the forecast assumed "the technology continuing to get better. And if GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such a major economic expansion".

Clark's remarks come as the company prepares for an initial public offering expected in November that could value the firm at up to $2 trillion.  HUMANS IN CONTROL, FOR NOW Clark issued a wake-up call to policymakers about the speed of AI development, saying there was growing evidence of a "singularity" where AI development outpaces human control. "We should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI but science as a whole will speed up, and this will feel confusing and disorienting, and will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril," he said in a lecture to hundreds of government and finance officials. AI was a major topic at the IMF and World Bank meetings, as both a source of growth offsetting high energy prices and a potential threat to stability if it falls short of its promise as a productivity game-changer and stock valuations crash.  Officials also expressed worries about AI destroying certain jobs and leaving some countries behind. But Clark, a former journalist who serves as Anthropic's "head of public benefit," painted a picture of a rosy future where AI was a force multiplier for scientific discovery, solving mathematical, engineering and biological problems, including new drug discovery, as human researchers are supplemented by hundreds or thousands of AI assistants.  More countries can participate in the AI revolution by helping to build the data center computing capacity needed to power AI, he said. STRICTEST CONTROLS ON BIOLOGICAL RESEARCH Clark cautioned that global leaders need to understand how powerful AI will become and make urgent choices about how to regulate the technology. "Being able to use AI for science opens us up to the misuses of science as well, biological and cyber weapons and things we cannot yet imagine, and we have many choices to make," he said. Biological research, where AI has already created new viruses, is an area "where we want the strictest human oversight and transparency to maintain safety." Despite some recent high-profile incidents where rogue AI systems have escaped testing environments and hacked websites and databases, he said AI was still under human control. But the window to impose safeguards was shrinking as AI became more capable and was now "a small number of years."  Clark also acknowledged that AI was causing job losses in some fields with "high AI exposure" such as call centers and customer service personnel. But for other fields, such as scientific research, he said AI was enhancing employment and a major unknown was its potential to create jobs in completely new industries.

Source: Reuters

item.title: Russia says it hit Ukrainian steel plants, power infrastructure and ships
item.description: Russia said on Saturday it had carried out a large-scale overnight attack on Ukrainian and infrastructure targets including the country's largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih, and vessels using the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia said on Saturday it had carried out a large-scale overnight attack on Ukrainian and infrastructure targets including the country's largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih, and vessels using the Ukrainian port of Odesa. The plant is owned by steel giant ArcelorMittal , which [USN:L1N45H03O TEXT:"suspended"] operations there in September after a series of Russian ballistic missile strikes. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a statement, Russia's defence ministry said the plant supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex. It said Russian forces had also hit an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr and another steel plant in Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front line. A cargo vessel in the Black Sea was also hit, the ministry said, alleging that it was delivering military cargo to Odesa. Later in the day, the ministry said Russian strikes during the afternoon had hit a vehicle-repair plant in Lutsk, an electricity substation in the western Ternopil region and another cargo vessel south of Odesa that it said was carrying military and dual-use cargo. Reuters could not independently confirm the ministry's reports.

item.title: 'Our land, our Albania': young lawmaker demands new future as protests rage
item.description: A young lawmaker demands as new future as protests rage in Tirana.
item.dc:creator: Fatos Bytyci
item.content:encoded: Marjana Koceku's life changed last year when Prime Minister Edi Rama hand-picked her to run for Albania's parliament, one of a legion of young lawmakers he hoped would become the face of his Socialist Party. This week, however, the 25-year-old, now an independent member of parliament, joined [USN:L1N4610AQ TEXT:"mass student protests"] calling for Rama to step down. Corruption, a lack of jobs and a general feeling that the government does not work for them have created a deep-seated anger that spilled over this week, when young protesters swarmed the capital Tirana, setting fire to government buildings and banks and hurling pavement stones at police. The government and the police have condemned the violence. According to police figures, 500 protestors have been detained, 330 of whom have been released. Some 120 police and 45 protesters have been injured, the figures show, although the protester figure is likely higher given that many injuries have gone unrecorded. Albania's unrest is part of a wave of student activism in Europe, including in France, where high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities. YOUTH PROTESTS THREATEN RAMA'S RULE "The country is amazing, but ... the wrong policies that have been implemented by this political elite are completely against what the Albanian communities and Albanian citizens have been asking and seeking for so long," Koceku said during the protests on Friday as police fired tear gas and water cannon at protesters nearby. Rama, a former basketball player, has been in power since 2013, half Koceku's life. He won a fourth term in elections last year but his administration has since been dogged by corruption scandals. Rama denies wrongdoing and this week told Reuters that he would not step down. "Governments are changed through democratic elections and we had them last year, not through violence," he said. Still, the protests represent the biggest threat to his rule yet. They follow months of mostly peaceful demonstrations sparked by plans to build a luxury resort on Albania's pristine southern coastline. The project, whose backers include US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, has faced legal challenges. Villagers told Reuters in July that their land was [USN:L6N42J18T TEXT:"wrongfully sold"] for the development. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was [USN:L6N4380FB TEXT:"wanted by prosecutors"] on suspicion of drug trafficking, accusations his lawyer denied. Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute. He did not respond to requests for comment. That was not the only controversy for Rama's government. Last year, prosecutors alleged that his deputy prime minister was involved in [USN:L6N3ZC0BA TEXT:"doling out construction contracts"] to favoured companies, charges Rama and the deputy deny. "I didn't agree, especially with the policies that they were implementing against nature, and our land and our Albania," Koceku said. This week, protesters said they had resorted to violence because they had not felt heard. The Kushner-backed project upset Koceku, who has a close relationship with the land. She is from the remote mountains of northern Albania where her family runs a small, no-frills guest house on the shore of a lake. "Our country is the Albanian people," she said, the air around her thick with acrid tear gas. "They create the future, they create the now, and they are the ones who can bring our country forward. Not a single person, not a single government."

item.title: インド警察、「ゴキブリ人民党」創設者を逮捕＝報道
item.description: [１７日 ロイター] -
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
[１７日 ロイター] - インドの複数のメディアは１７日、若者中心の団体「ゴキブリ人民党（ＣＪＰ）」の創設者アビジート・ディプケ氏が警察に逮捕されたと報じた。

テレビ局ＮＤＴＶとインディア・トゥデーによると、ディプケ氏は治安の混乱を防ぐために逮捕され、１７日に特別行政治安判事の前に出頭する予定だ。

同氏は拘束されたＣＪＰ幹部２人を支援するため、１６日にデリーで抗議集会を開くよう呼びかけていた。集会には数百人が参加し、国旗を振って選挙管理委員長の辞任を求めた。

ディプケ氏は１６日、デリー中心部の住宅から出たところを拘束され、短い口論の後、パトカーに押し込まれて連れ去られた。警察はこれに先立ち、ディプケ氏と面会し、抗議活動を実施しないよう警告していた。

item.title: ソフトバンクＧ、米警備大手アライド買収検討＝関係筋
item.description:
Milana Vinn
[１６日 ロイター] - ソフトバンクグループが米警備サービス大手アライド・ユニバーサルの...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
ソフトバンクＧ、米警備大手アライド買収検討＝関係筋 10/17 15:08 配信

ソフトバンクグループのロゴ。９月東京で撮影。REUTERS/Manami Yamada

Milana Vinn

[１６日 ロイター] - ソフトバンクグループが米警備サービス大手アライド・ユニバーサルの買収を検討している。関係者が１６日明らかにした。買収案では、アライドの評価額が約１８０億ドルになる可能性がある。

アライドは企業や各種施設、大規模イベントに警備員を派遣する事業を手がける。データセンター分野でも事業を拡大しており、施設の開発と運営の両面を支援している。

ソフトバンクはアライドの買収が実現すれば、特定の警備業務で人員の一部をいずれロボットに置き換えることを目指す。ただ人型ロボットの警備業務への導入には長い時間がかかるとみられる。

買収検討は初期段階にあり、買収額を含め、最終決定には至っていないという。

ロイター 関連ニュース アングル：ＡＩ関連の資金調達、低格付け領域にも拡大　投資家は警戒感強める コラム：ベセント氏の危うい賭け、ＡＩ主導の経済成長は「債務病」の特効薬ならず コラム：進む米中デカップリング、中国「保有米国債」の脅威減退か コラム：オープンＡＩ投資で膨らむソフトバンクの財務リスク コラム：孫氏、オープンＡＩへ300億ドル追加投資か　際立つ「一点張り」 最終更新: 10/17(土) 15:08 ロイター

item.title: Strong dollar, weak hand for Trump before midterms
item.description: A surging dollar is exposing a central contradiction in President Trump's economic agenda: currency markets are delivering the opposite of what his administration wants.
item.dc:creator: Jamie McGeever
item.content:encoded: With the US midterm elections weeks away, a surging dollar is exposing a central contradiction in President Donald Trump's economic agenda: currency markets are delivering the opposite of what his administration wants. Trump's economic record in the first two years of his second term is being heavily scrutinized. Polls show voters' approval of his handling of the economy has rarely been lower. That goes a long way toward explaining why [USN:L4N45Y17K TEXT:"betting markets "]point to his Republican Party losing control of the House of Representatives, and perhaps even the Senate, on November 3. Yet if there's any truth to the market adage that a country's currency is a reflection of the world's confidence in its economy, Trump should be going into the upcoming vote brimming with confidence. The dollar (.DXY) has been rising steadily, recently hitting its [USN:L4N46001K TEXT:"strongest level in 18 months"] against major peers. But a strong and appreciating exchange rate is the last thing Trump wants. His administration's economic and trade policies are aiming to revive US manufacturing, make American exports great again and shrink the trade deficit. A strengthening currency won't help with any of that. WRONG DIRECTION One might expect the dollar to be under pressure, especially given that the [USN:L1N45R0RR TEXT:"US trade balance"] has not narrowed according to the administration's plan. Imports have exploded to record levels, largely driven by US companies hoovering up the chips, equipment and goods needed for the AI build-out , and the country's trade deficit is widening. It was [USN:L1N45F0L5 TEXT:"2.7% of gross domestic product"] earlier this year — one of the smallest readings of the century — but it could be headed for 4% of GDP next year, according to Dean Maki at hedge fund Point72. But the dollar is not weakening. It did during Trump's first year back in the Oval Office, amid concerns about [USN:L1N44H0RB TEXT:""dollar debasement""] and a "sell America" mentality among foreign investors fostered by Trump's tariffs , but that has since gone into reverse. Why? Because exchange rates are relative, and the greenback currently appears to be the proverbial "cleanest dirty shirt." While the US is suffering from acute debt and deficit concerns, so are other developed countries, most [USN:S8N50E09F TEXT:"notably France"]. Investors fear that Paris is unwilling to take the politically unpalatable steps to get its budget under control and are thus slamming the euro . Similarly, worries that higher interest rates will make it nearly impossible for Japan to service its [USN:SPN45900X TEXT:"enormous debt load"] have anchored the yen near its recent historical lows. In short, the dollar is "winning" as much by default as it is benefiting from the flood of global capital chasing the US AI dream. This is not what the White House had in mind. Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent clearly [USN:L8N3YR24M TEXT:"want a weaker dollar"], even if decades of a quasi-official "strong dollar" policy at the White House — dating back to the days of former Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin in the 1990s — make it challenging for them to say so outright. The Trump administration's views on the US currency were flagged almost exactly two years ago in "A User’s Guide to Restructuring the Global Trading System," a paper by Stephen Miran, then a senior strategist at hedge fund Hudson Bay Capital Management. Miran went on to serve as chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers under Trump, who later appointed him as a Federal Reserve governor for a short spell. He has since returned to HBC, but his 41-page manual still appears to serve as a broad framework for the administration's trade, currency and economic policy. The blueprint has come to be known as the "Mar-a-Lago Accord," in a nod to the famous 1985 "Plaza Accord," under which the world's leading economic powers agreed to devalue the dollar. Echoing Trump's decades-long view, Miran wrote that "deep unhappiness with the prevailing economic order is rooted in persistent overvaluation of the dollar ... (which) makes US exports less competitive, US imports cheaper, and handicaps American manufacturing." He has a point. At the time of Trump's inauguration in January last year, the dollar's broad, real effective exchange rate was the strongest in over 30 years. Miran argues that the global trade and financial systems can be rewired to America's benefit, but the path "is narrow, and will require careful planning, precise execution, and attention to steps to minimize adverse consequences." Americans casting their midterm election votes on November 3 may not have the patience for this. While the US economy continues to grow at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, households are feeling the adverse economic consequences of Trump's policies over the past two years. Tariffs have raised the cost of imported goods, according to a recent New York Fed study , and the US war with Iran, launched in February, has led to soaring energy costs, most notably record-high diesel prices at the pump. As a consequence, inflation remains elevated, bond yields are the highest in a quarter of a century, and real wages are now falling. Given all this, the big question is whether the American public will give the Trump administration the space to try to turn the dollar's tide. A FAREWELL TO MULTILATERALISM Efforts to reverse the dollar's march higher will be challenging, to put it mildly. History suggests that what's needed is multilateral, globally coordinated action, but that is the antithesis of Trump's "America First" worldview. Piecemeal and bilateral actions, like the Treasury's recent [USN:L4N45304A TEXT:"intervention with Japan"] to support the yen , are likely too small to have any lasting impact. Further interventions cannot be ruled out if the dollar continues to strengthen. For example, when writing about the yen, Stephen Jen, CEO of Eurizon SLJ Asset Management, recently argued that a series of targeted, surprise "mini" interventions could chip away at the dollar without triggering an avalanche of depreciation, helping the Trump administration meet its foreign exchange and wider goals over time. "The Trump Administration ... wants to find ways to guide the dollar lower. This is needed because, in order for the US to attain economic security, it needs to reclaim a certain level of manufacturing self-sufficiency. To do that, a weaker dollar would be necessary. The challenge, of course, is to guide the dollar lower without spooking the capital markets," Jen wrote in May. Much will depend on the frequency and size of such moves. Official action to weaken the dollar against major currencies is rare. Before this year's yen intervention, the last time US and Japanese authorities coordinated to sell dollars against the yen was in 1998. The Fed intervened with the European Central Bank and other authorities to support the euro, but that was back in late 2000, just after the single currency's launch. Since the era of free-floating exchange rates began in the early 1970s, when President Richard Nixon took the US off the gold standard, there have only been two truly global efforts to force a change in the dollar's broad value. Both were in the 1980s: the Plaza Accord in 1985 to lower what was an extremely elevated dollar, and the Louvre Accord in 1987 to essentially take the sting out of Plaza. These accords were products of their time. The dollar is nowhere near as strong as it was back then, and that was an era when multilateral cooperation was still in vogue. As the country looks set to enter the final two years of the Trump era, the dollar's relative strength could say much about how much of his economic agenda he has been able to achieve since first entering the White House almost 10 years ago. (The opinions expressed here are those of the author, a columnist for Reuters) Enjoying this column? Check out Reuters Open Interest (ROI), your essential new source for global financial commentary.
